fetched_contents.text: Durability of Concrete Made with Coal Bottom Ash Portland Cements Abstract Highlights What are the main findings? * The standardization of coal bottom ash (CBA) as a cement constituent contributes to climate change mitigation. * Coal bottom ash (Z) is included as a new constituent in the EU Standardization Request published on 28 July 2025. * For the first time, the durability of Z-concretes is assessed by the depth of penetration of water under pressure test. * Clinker factor reduction with newly standardized constituents decreases the near- zero cement cost (~500 €/t). * CEM II/B-Z and CEM II/C-M concretes meet water penetration requirements for all exposure classes. Abstract The Portland cement industry, responsible for approximately 7.4% of global anthropogenic carbon dioxide emissions, must balance rising cement demand with ambitious greenhouse gas reduction targets. In parallel, the rapid accumulation of industrial solid waste highlights the need for effective valorization routes. Reducing the clinker factor remains a powerful measure to mitigate climate impacts in the cement sector. This study evaluates the durability of concretes made with ground coal bottom ash (CBA), a newly standardized Portland cement constituent, using the depth of penetration of water under pressure test (EN 12390-8). The experimental results show that concretes produced with CEM II/B-Z and CEM II/C-M cements meet both average (≤30 mm) and maximum (≤50 mm) water penetration criteria for mass, reinforced, and prestressed concrete across all EN 206-1 exposure classes. Concretes made with CEM VI (S-L) and CEM VI (S-Z) comply for XS1, XS2, XD, XA1, XM, and XF classes. However, for XS3, XA2, and XA3, compliance (≤20 mm and ≤30 mm) is not achieved when using mix design B (300 kg/m3, w/c = 0.50). These findings provide robust technical evidence supporting CBA as a viable cement constituent that enhances durability while enabling clinker factor reduction. Keywords: climate change mitigation, IPCC, blended cements, coal bottom ash, building materials, cement, Roadmap 2050, policy 1. Introduction Portland cement is the second largest carbon dioxide-emitting industrial sector, generating 7.4% [1] of global anthropogenic emissions, but concrete (made by mixing Portland cement, aggregates, water and chemical admixtures) is the second most used material in the world after water. In addition, demand for Portland cement could increase by up to 45% by 2050 [2], risking a rise in carbon dioxide emissions. Since it is a hard-to-abate sector, carbon capture use and storage (CCUS) techniques are essential to the net-zero or near-zero pathways for Portland cement, but reducing the clinker factor (clinker/cement ratio) could play a supporting role. Clinker production at high temperatures (>1450 °C) is the highest CO2 emission process (around 85%) in cement manufacturing, mainly from burning fossil fuels (pet coke, diesel, etc.) and the limestone calcination process (Table 1). Accordingly, minimizing the clinker factor (clinker/cement ratio) to manufacture low-clinker cement is the most effective procedure to produce low-carbon cements. Table 1. Therefore, the reduction in the clinker factor is a cheaper supporting measure for the mitigation of climate change [3]. Nevertheless, the low availability of traditional Portland cement constituents, primarily coal fly ash or blast-furnace slag, is perceived as the major limitation in implementing this measure for the development of low-carbon cements, because of the phase-out of coal-fired power plants and the change in steel production from blast furnace–basic oxygen furnace (BF-BOF) technology to electric arc furnaces (EAFs) with direct reduced iron (DRI) made with green hydrogen, which is currently available [4]. Consequently, new Portland cement constituents should be explored and standardized in order to encourage widespread usage. Current Portland cement constituents act in the cementitious system as fillers, promoting clinker phase hydration (limestone), or as pozzolanic and/or hydraulic materials (coal fly ash, ground granulated blast-furnace slag, natural pozzolana, calcined clay, and so on) [5]. When latent hydraulic materials are ground finely, it dramatically increases the surface area and may react with water in the presence of CaO (calcareous coal fly ash and ground granulated blast-furnace slag—high-Ca aluminosilicates) [5]. By contrast, pozzolanic materials, especially high-Si aluminosilicates (siliceous coal fly ash, natural and calcined pozzolana, siliceous coal bottom ash, etc.), can react with calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)2) and water to form C-S-H gel [6]. In the course of this century, many feasibility studies have been launched for the usage of natural and waste resources as new Portland cement constituents. Climate change mitigation and circular economy goals have caused intense research activity in this field. Nevertheless, some potential Portland cement constituents that fulfill all the technical and economic criteria cannot be used since they are not standardized or do not fit existing construction product standards. Abstract Recent coal-fired power plant closures resulted in limited availability of fresh fly ash in some regions of the United States of America. This combined with stricter environmental regulations has led to national specifications being modified to allow the use of coal bottom ash in addition to coal fly ash as a supplementary cementitious material in making concrete. Coal bottom ash is different from coal fly ash in its chemical, physical and mineralogical composition. The literature review conducted in this study identified variability in performance of coal ash that can be related to variability in the available sources of the collected coal ash; namely, landfills, lagoons or freshly collected bottom ash. The findings indicate that the work is needed to ensure consistent performance of coal ash collected from variable sources. It is recommended that a study on coal ash performance be initiated to ensure adequate and consistent performance and durability of structural concrete elements in the state of Florida using coal ash as a supplementary material. 17. fetched_contents.text: Coal Fly Ash - User Guideline - Portland Cement Concrete - User Guidelines for Waste and Byproduct Materials in Pavement Construction COAL FLY ASH User Guideline ---------------------------------------- Portland Cement Concrete INTRODUCTION Coal fly ash has been successfully used in Portland cement concrete (PCC) as a mineral admixture, and more recently as a component of blended cement, for nearly 60 years. As an admixture, fly ash functions as either a partial replacement for, or an addition to, Portland cement and is added directly into ready-mix concrete at the batch plant. Fly ash can also be interground with cement clinker or blended with Portland cement to produce blended cements. ASTM C595(1) defines two blended cement products in which fly ash has been added: 1) Portland-pozzolan cement (Type IP), containing 15 to 40 percent pozzolan, or 2) Pozzolan modified Portland cement (Type I-PM), containing less than 15 percent pozzolan. ASTM C618 defines two classes of fly ash for use in concrete: 1) Class F, usually derived from the burning of anthracite or bituminous coal, and 2) Class C, usually derived from the burning of lignite or subbituminous coal.(2) ASTM C618 also delineates requirements for the physical, chemical, and mechanical properties for these two classes of fly ash. Class F fly ash is pozzolanic, with little or no cementing value alone. Class C fly ash has self-cementing properties as well as pozzolanic properties. PERFORMANCE RECORD A 1992 survey of all 50 state transportation agencies indicated that 40 states have had experience in the use of fly ash as a mineral admixture in concrete, usually as a partial replacement for Portland cement, although a number of states have also used blended Portland-pozzolan cement. Virtually all 40 of these states have used fly ash in concrete pavements and shoulders. This same survey indicated that 44 states had specifications for the use of fly ash as a partial replacement for Portland cement in concrete.(3) At the time of this survey, at least eight states did not permit the use of fly ash in either bridge deck or structural concrete. A number of states also did not permit the use of fly ash in white concrete items, such as curbs, sidewalks, and median barriers, and two states (Arkansas and New Mexico) reported questionable performance experience: Arkansas had temporarily discontinued the use of fly ash in bridge deck concrete, and New Mexico had a temporary moratorium on the use of Class C fly ash in concrete, pending further investigation.(4) The principal benefits ascribed to the use of fly ash in concrete include enhanced workability due to spherical fly ash particles, reduced bleeding and less water demand, increased ultimate strength, reduced permeability and chloride ion penetration, lower heat of hydration, greater resistance to sulfate attack, greater resistance to alkali-aggregate reactivity, and reduced drying shrinkage.(5) The main precautions usually associated with the use of fly ash in concrete include somewhat slower early strength development, extended initial setting time, possible difficulty in controlling air content, seasonal limitations during winter months, and quality control of fly ash sources.(5) The use of Class F fly ash usually results in slower early strength development, but the use of Class C fly ash does not and may even enhance early strength development. MATERIAL PROCESSING REQUIREMENTS Source Control To ensure the quality of fly ash for use in PCC, the following sources of ash should be avoided: * Ash from a peaking plant instead of a base loaded plant. * Ash from plants burning different coals or blends of coal. * Ash from plants burning other fuels (wood chips, tires, trash) blended with coal. * Ash from plants using oil as a supplementary fuel. * Ash from plants using precipitator additives, such as ammonia. * Ash from start-up or shut-down phases of operation. * Ash from plants not operating at a "steady state." * Ash that is handled and stored using a wet system. The net result of all these restrictions is that only a relatively low percentage (25 to 30 percent, at most) of all the coal fly ash produced annually is even potentially suitable for use in PCC. Drying or Conditioning When used in blended cement or as a partial replacement for Portland cement in ready-mix concrete, fly ash must be in a dry form and as such requires no processing. When used as a raw feed material for the production of Portland cement, either dry or conditioned ash can be used. Quality Control Fly ash used in concrete should be as consistent and uniform as possible. Fly ash to be used in concrete should be monitored by a quality assurance/quality control (QA/QC) program that complies with the recommended procedures in ASTM C311.(6) These procedures establish standards for methods of sampling and frequency of performing tests for fineness, loss on ignition (LOI), specific gravity, and pozzolanic activity such that the consistency of a fly ash source can be certified. Many state transportation agencies, through their own program of sampling and testing, have been able to prequalify sources of fly ash within their own state (or from nearby states) for acceptance in ready-mixed concrete. Prequalification of fly ashes from different sources provides an agency with a certain level of confidence in the event fly ashes from different sources are to be used in the same project. ENGINEERING PROPERTIES Some of the engineering properties of fly ash that are of particular interest when fly ash is used as an admixture or a cement addition to PCC mixes include fineness, LOI, chemical composition, moisture content, and pozzolanic activity. Most specifying agencies refer to ASTM C618(2) when citing acceptance criteria for the use of fly ash in concrete. Chemical and functional contribution of coal ash to cement/concrete

Coal ash contributes to cement and concrete primarily through its pozzolanic and, in some cases, cementitious activity, driven by reactive silica and alumina in its chemical composition. The evidence indicates that coal ash is often classified into two broad types for cementitious applications: Class F and Class C. Class F ash is generally derived from anthracite or bituminous coal and is pozzolanic, with little or no cementing value alone, whereas Class C ash is derived from lignite or subbituminous coal and has self-cementing properties in addition to pozzolanic properties [N5-F1]. This classification is also reflected in broader industrial practice, where coal fly ash is broadly classified into Class C and Class F based on chemical composition, and bottom ash can meet the Class F or Class C classification under ASTM C618 [N6-R3][N6-R4]. The evidence further states that ASTM C618 defines coal fly ash and raw or calcined natural pozzolan for use in concrete where cementitious or pozzolanic action, or both, is desired [N5-R2][N5-F2]. This means that coal ash can act either as a supplementary cementitious material (SCM) or as a pozzolanic admixture, depending on its type and processing.

The chemical components that drive this activity are primarily silica (SiO₂), alumina (Al₂O₃), and calcium oxide (CaO), which are present in the ash and enable pozzolanic reactions with calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)₂) and water to form calcium silicate hydrate (C-S-H) gel [N5-F1]. The evidence also points to reactive silica content as a key factor in pozzolanic activity, with high reactive silica content and satisfactory levels of other components contributing to high pozzolanic activity [N1-R2]. The same evidence notes that coal bottom ash can be used in Portland cement, and that pozzolanic properties of ground coal bottom ash and coal fly ash cements were investigated to assess their pozzolanic performance [N1-R3]. This supports the conclusion that the functional contribution of coal ash is rooted in its ability to participate in hydration reactions that generate cementitious products, even if the ash itself is not fully hydraulic by itself.

In terms of hydration, early-age behavior, and long-term strength, coal ash tends to modify hydration by slowing early strength development and extending initial setting time, especially when used as a mineral admixture or partial replacement for cement. The evidence from ASTM C618 and the FHWA user guideline notes that the use of Class F fly ash usually results in slower early strength development, while Class C fly ash may not and may even enhance early strength development [N5-F1]. The durability study on coal bottom ash Portland cements found that concretes produced with CEM II/B-Z and CEM II/C-M cements met water penetration requirements for mass, reinforced, and prestressed concrete across all EN 206-1 exposure classes, indicating that coal ash can support durability without sacrificing the ability to meet strength and exposure criteria [N2-F3]. The same study also shows that the standardization of coal bottom ash as a cement constituent contributes to climate change mitigation and enables clinker factor reduction, which can improve long-term performance by lowering the environmental footprint of cement production [N2-F3]. Thus, coal ash can improve long-term strength and durability by substituting some clinker and reducing the amount of cement required, while still maintaining adequate hydration and structural performance.

Regarding concrete workability, shrinkage, and durability, the evidence points to several performance benefits. Coal ash is reported to enhance workability due to its spherical particle shape, reduce bleeding and water demand, and lower heat of hydration, which can improve early-age behavior and reduce cracking risk [N5-F1]. It also increases ultimate strength, reduces permeability and chloride ion penetration, lowers drying shrinkage, and improves resistance to sulfate attack and alkali-aggregate reactivity [N5-F1]. The durability study on coal bottom ash concrete found that CBA-based concretes met water penetration requirements for all exposure classes and that clinker factor reduction improved durability while enabling near-zero cement cost savings [N2-F3]. The evidence also highlights that coal bottom ash can be used in structural concrete and that coal ash can improve the strength and durability of products using it [N3-R3]. Overall, coal ash modifies concrete in a favorable direction by improving workability, reducing shrinkage, and enhancing resistance to environmental degradation, which collectively contribute to more durable concrete structures.

In summary, coal ash’s chemical and functional contribution to cement and concrete is mainly through its silica-alumina content and its ability to participate in pozzolanic or cementitious reactions, especially in Class C ash, which can also have self-cementing properties [N5-F1][N6-R3][N6-R4]. It affects hydration by slowing early-age development in Class F ash and potentially enhancing early strength in Class C ash, and it supports long-term strength and durability by reducing permeability, chloride penetration, and drying shrinkage while meeting exposure-class requirements [N5-F1][N2-F3]. Its effects on concrete workability, shrinkage, and durability are generally favorable: improved workability, reduced shrinkage, and enhanced durability [N5-F1][N3-R3].

Benefits of coal ash use in cement and concrete production

The use of coal ash in cement and concrete production offers clear cost, supply, environmental, and performance advantages. On the cost and supply side, coal ash is often viewed as a lower-cost alternative to raw materials because it is a byproduct of coal combustion rather than a primary ingredient. The evidence states that the use of alternative material such as fly ash can help reduce environmental impacts and that significant impacts reductions are associated with cement production, while reusing fly ash helps reduce environmental impacts and can reduce the cost of disposal [N3-R1][N3-R3]. The durability study on coal bottom ash concrete also notes that the standardization of coal bottom ash as a cement constituent contributes to climate change mitigation and can reduce near-zero cement cost by about 500 €/t, indicating a substantial cost advantage in some applications [N2-F3]. This makes coal ash attractive not only as a waste stream but also as a way to lower material costs and improve the economic viability of concrete production.

Environmentally, the benefits are strong. Coal ash reuse reduces the need for landfill disposal and helps mitigate climate change by lowering the carbon footprint of cement production. The evidence explicitly links fly ash reuse to reduced greenhouse gas emissions, reduced disposal costs, and improved strength and durability [N3-R3]. It also states that turning liabilities into opportunities highlights the region’s use of coal ash to reduce the carbon footprint, and that harvested ash can provide environmental benefits for all harvesting processes evaluated [N3-R2][N3-R5]. The durability study similarly emphasizes that coal bottom ash is included as a new constituent in the EU Standardization Request, supporting climate change mitigation and the development of low-carbon cements [N2-F3]. Taken together, these sources show that coal ash reuse is a major environmental win: it diverts waste from landfills, reduces emissions, and supports circular economy goals.

Performance benefits are also significant. Coal ash improves concrete durability by reducing permeability, chloride ion penetration, sulfate attack, and alkali-aggregate reactivity, while also reducing drying shrinkage and heat of hydration [N5-F1]. The durability study on coal bottom ash concrete found that CBA-based concretes met water penetration requirements for all exposure classes, which is a strong indicator of long-term durability [N2-F3]. The evidence also states that coal ash can improve the strength and durability of products using it [N3-R3], and that replacing cement with harvested ash provides environmental benefits for all harvesting processes evaluated [N3-R5]. These performance advantages are important because they mean that coal ash can be used to produce more durable, less permeable concrete without compromising strength or exposure-class compliance.

In addition, coal ash can support the development of low-clinker cement. The durability study notes that reducing the clinker factor is a cheaper supporting measure for climate change mitigation, and that coal bottom ash can be used in blended cements to achieve this goal [N2-F3]. This aligns with the broader evidence that coal ash can be used as a cementitious or pozzolanic constituent, with ASTM C618 covering both pozzolanic and cementitious action, or both [N5-R2][N5-F2]. In practical terms, this means coal ash can help meet sustainability targets while still delivering concrete that is strong, durable, and structurally sound.

Overall, the benefits of coal ash use in cement and concrete are substantial: cost savings through lower material and disposal expenses, environmental advantages from waste reuse and reduced emissions, and performance improvements such as enhanced durability, reduced permeability, and improved workability [N3-R1][N3-R3][N5-F1][N2-F3]. These benefits make coal ash an attractive and increasingly important material in modern cementitious systems.

Processing challenges and practical constraints of coal ash

Processing coal ash in cement/concrete is constrained by variability in composition, contamination risks, and technical limitations in blending, curing, and quality control. One major issue is the variability in coal ash composition, which can significantly influence how fly ash behaves as a supplementary cementitious material. The evidence from the Florida structural concrete evaluation notes that variability in mineralogy and chemical composition can significantly influence coal ash behavior [N4-F4]. This variability is important because it affects consistency and performance across different sources, requiring careful specification and quality control to ensure reliable results.

Contamination risks are another major constraint. The same Florida evaluation report states that landfilled or ponded fly ash can be comingled with bottom ash, flue-gas desulfurization materials (FGD), and fluidized bed combustion (FBC) fly ashes, which can increase sulfur content and other impurities [N4-F4]. It also warns that the form of sulfur present in harvested coal ash, such as calcium sulfate, calcium sulfite, or sodium/alkali sulfate, can substantially affect performance, even though ASTM C618’s chemical analyses do not identify the form of sulfur [N4-F4]. Excess alkali content is also noted as a concern because it can affect reaction rates and concrete durability [N4-F4]. This means that coal ash processing must be carefully managed to avoid contamination from non-ash materials and to ensure that the chemical composition remains within acceptable limits for cementitious use.

The evidence also points to practical handling requirements. ASTM C618 and related guidance emphasize that coal ash sources should be controlled to avoid ash from peaking plants, blended coal, other fuels, precipitator additives, start-up/shutdown phases, wet handling, and non-steady-state operation [N5-F1]. These restrictions are intended to ensure quality and consistency. The FHWA user guideline adds that only a relatively low percentage of all coal fly ash produced annually is potentially suitable for use in PCC because of these source restrictions [N5-F1]. This highlights a key processing challenge: even though coal ash is abundant, only a fraction is suitable for cement/concrete use due to inconsistent sources and handling conditions.

Blending and quality control are also technically limited. The FHWA guidance notes that fly ash used in concrete should be as consistent and uniform as possible and should be monitored by a QA/QC program that tests fineness, loss on ignition, specific gravity, and pozzolanic activity [N5-F1]. It further states that prequalification of fly ash sources is important to ensure consistency across projects, because fly ash from different sources may behave differently [N5-F1]. The durability study on coal bottom ash concrete also emphasizes the need for standardization and the role of exposure-class compliance in concrete performance [N2-F3]. These points show that coal ash processing is not simply a matter of mixing; it requires careful selection, conditioning, testing, and quality assurance to ensure consistent performance.

In addition, processing conditions can affect the effectiveness of coal ash. The evidence indicates that drying or conditioning is required for blended cement or ready-mix concrete, and that moisture content can influence entrained air content and air-entraining requirements [N5-F1]. It also notes that finely divided materials may reduce entrained air content, so air content must be maintained through tests and additional admixtures if needed [N5-F1]. This means that coal ash processing must be matched to the concrete mix design and curing conditions to avoid adverse effects on workability and durability.

Overall, the processing challenges of coal ash are substantial: variability in composition can reduce consistency, contamination risks can degrade performance, and technical limitations in blending, curing, and quality control are necessary to ensure reliable use [N4-F4][N5-F1]. These constraints must be managed through careful source control, conditioning, testing, and standardization to maximize the benefits of coal ash in cement and concrete.

Industry standards and typical specifications for coal ash in cementitious materials

Industry standards for coal ash in cementitious materials are primarily governed by ASTM C618, which defines acceptable coal ash types and specifies the requirements for cementitious or pozzolanic action. The evidence states that ASTM C618 covers coal fly ash and raw or calcined natural pozzolan for use in concrete where cementitious or pozzolanic action, or both, is desired [N5-R2][N5-F2]. It also defines two classes of fly ash for use in concrete: Class F, usually derived from anthracite or bituminous coal, and Class C, usually derived from lignite or subbituminous coal [N5-F1][N6-R5]. This classification is central to specification because it determines which ash types are suitable for different applications.

The standard also sets physical and chemical requirements for the materials, and specifies testing for fineness, strength activity index, water requirement, soundness, and autoclave expansion or contraction [N5-F2]. These tests are used to ensure that the ash meets the necessary performance criteria for use in concrete. ASTM C618 also excludes certain residues such as those from fluidized bed combustion, burning of municipal solid waste or other refuse with coal, or burning of industrial or municipal solid waste in incinerators [N5-F2]. This exclusion is important because it limits the scope of acceptable coal ash to those that are chemically and physically compatible with cementitious use.

The standard’s requirements affect specification, grading, and use limits in several ways. First, ASTM C618 distinguishes between pozzolanic and cementitious action, which means that different ash types may be used for different applications. Class F ash is pozzolanic, with little or no cementing value alone, while Class C ash has self-cementing properties in addition to pozzolanic properties [N5-F1][N6-R5]. Second, the standard requires consistent and uniform material, with quality control through sampling, testing, and prequalification programs [N5-F1]. This means that specification is not only about chemical composition but also about batch-to-batch consistency and source reliability. Third, the standard’s limits on chemical composition and physical properties define acceptable use limits, including limits on SO₃ content and other impurities, which are important for avoiding harmful effects on concrete performance [N4-F4].

In addition to ASTM C618, the evidence indicates that coal ash can be used in blended cement. ASTM C595 defines blended cement products in which fly ash has been added, including Portland-pozzolan cement (Type IP) and Pozzolan modified Portland cement (Type I-PM), with specified percentages of pozzolan [N5-F1]. This shows that the standard framework extends beyond raw ash to blended cement applications, reinforcing the idea that coal ash is regulated not only by its chemical and physical properties but also by how it is incorporated into cementitious systems.

The broader evidence also supports the importance of classification for specification. Coal fly ash is classified into Class C and Class F based on chemical composition, and bottom ash can meet the Class F or Class C classification under ASTM C618 [N6-R3][N6-R4]. This classification is useful for specifying which ash type is suitable for a given mix and for predicting its behavior in concrete. It also explains why ASTM C618 is so important: it provides a common language for specifying acceptable ash types, acceptable action, and acceptable performance.

In conclusion, ASTM C618 and related standards define coal ash as a material for cementitious or pozzolanic action, or both, and classify it into Class F and Class C based on source and chemical composition [N5-R2][N5-F2][N6-R5]. The standards set physical and chemical requirements, test procedures, and exclusion criteria, which together determine specification, grading, and use limits [N5-F2]. They also support blended cement applications and emphasize consistency, source control, and quality assurance, ensuring that coal ash can be used reliably in cementitious materials [N5-F1][N5-F2].

# Integrated final answer: how coal ash contributes to cement and concrete, and its benefits and processing challenges

Coal ash is a key industrial byproduct that contributes to cement and concrete production through its chemical and functional properties. Its main contribution is via **pozzolanic activity** and, in some cases, **cementitious activity**, which together allow it to replace part of the cement content in concrete and improve performance. The evidence is clear that coal ash is classified into two broad types for cementitious applications: **Class F** and **Class C**, with Class F typically derived from anthracite or bituminous coal and Class C from lignite or subbituminous coal [N5-F1][N6-R5]. ASTM C618 is the central standard governing coal ash in cementitious materials, and it defines coal fly ash and raw or calcined natural pozzolan for use in concrete where **cementitious or pozzolanic action**, or both, is desired [N5-R2][N5-F2]. This classification and standardization framework is important because it determines which ash types are suitable for which applications and how they should be specified.

## 1) How coal ash chemically and functionally contributes to cement/concrete

### Chemical components driving activity
Coal ash’s contribution comes primarily from **reactive silica (SiO₂), alumina (Al₂O₃), and calcium oxide (CaO)**, which enable pozzolanic reactions with calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)₂) and water to form calcium silicate hydrate (C-S-H) gel [N5-F1]. The evidence also emphasizes that reactive silica content is a key driver of pozzolanic activity, with high reactive silica content and satisfactory levels of other components contributing to high pozzolanic activity [N1-R2]. This means that the ash itself is not always fully hydraulic, but it can still participate in cementitious reactions that improve concrete performance.

### Functional roles in hydration and long-term strength
Coal ash modifies hydration behavior in several ways. In practice, **Class F fly ash usually results in slower early strength development**, while **Class C fly ash may not and may even enhance early strength development** [N5-F1]. The durability study on coal bottom ash concrete found that concretes produced with CEM II/B-Z and CEM II/C-M cements met water penetration requirements for mass, reinforced, and prestressed concrete across all EN 206-1 exposure classes, indicating that coal ash can support durability without sacrificing exposure-class compliance [N2-F3]. The study also showed that the standardization of coal bottom ash as a cement constituent contributes to **climate change mitigation** and enables **clinker factor reduction**, which improves long-term performance by lowering the environmental footprint of cement production [N2-F3]. In other words, coal ash can improve long-term strength and durability by substituting some clinker and reducing cement demand, while still maintaining adequate hydration and structural performance.

### Effects on concrete workability, shrinkage, and durability
The evidence points to several favorable effects on concrete properties. Coal ash is reported to enhance **workability** due to its spherical particle shape, reduce **bleeding** and **water demand**, and lower **heat of hydration**, which can improve early-age behavior and reduce cracking risk [N5-F1]. It also increases **ultimate strength**, reduces **permeability** and **chloride ion penetration**, lowers **drying shrinkage**, and improves resistance to **sulfate attack** and **alkali-aggregate reactivity** [N5-F1]. The durability study further found that **coal bottom ash concrete met water penetration requirements for all exposure classes**, showing that coal ash can improve durability while meeting structural performance criteria [N2-F3]. In addition, the evidence states that coal ash can improve the strength and durability of products using it, and that replacing cement with harvested ash provides environmental benefits [N3-R3]. Taken together, these effects mean coal ash modifies concrete in a favorable direction: improved workability, reduced shrinkage, and enhanced durability.

## 2) Benefits of coal ash use in cement and concrete production

### Cost and supply advantages
One of the main benefits of coal ash is that it is often a **lower-cost alternative** to raw materials because it is a byproduct of coal combustion rather than a primary ingredient. The evidence notes that fly ash reuse can help reduce environmental impacts, and that reusing fly ash can reduce environmental impacts and lower the cost of disposal [N3-R1][N3-R3]. The durability study on coal bottom ash concrete also highlights that standardization of coal bottom ash as a cement constituent can reduce near-zero cement cost by about 500 €/t, showing a substantial cost advantage [N2-F3]. This makes coal ash attractive not only as a waste stream but also as a way to lower material costs and improve the economic viability of concrete production.

### Environmental benefits
Coal ash reuse offers strong environmental benefits. It reduces the need for **landfill disposal**, helps mitigate **climate change**, and supports **circular economy goals**. The evidence explicitly links fly ash reuse to reduced greenhouse gas emissions, reduced disposal costs, and improved strength and durability [N3-R3]. It also states that **turning liabilities into opportunities** highlights the use of coal ash to reduce the carbon footprint, and that harvested ash can provide environmental benefits for all harvesting processes evaluated [N3-R2][N3-R5]. The durability study similarly emphasizes that coal bottom ash is included in the EU Standardization Request and supports climate change mitigation and low-carbon cement development [N2-F3]. These benefits are particularly important because they show that coal ash can simultaneously reduce emissions, lower waste management costs, and support sustainable construction.

### Performance benefits
Performance benefits are also significant. Coal ash improves concrete durability by reducing **permeability**, **chloride ion penetration**, **sulfate attack**, and **alkali-aggregate reactivity**, while also reducing **drying shrinkage** and **heat of hydration** [N5-F1]. The durability study on coal bottom ash concrete found that CBA-based concretes met water penetration requirements for all exposure classes, which is a strong indicator of long-term durability [N2-F3]. The evidence also notes that coal ash can improve the strength and durability of products using it [N3-R3], and that replacing cement with harvested ash provides environmental benefits [N3-R5]. These performance advantages are important because they mean that coal ash can be used to produce more durable, less permeable concrete without compromising strength or exposure-class compliance.

### Support for low-clinker cement
A related benefit is that coal ash can help support the development of **low-clinker cement**. The durability study notes that reducing the clinker factor is a cheaper supporting measure for climate change mitigation, and that coal bottom ash can be used in blended cements to achieve this goal [N2-F3]. This aligns with the broader evidence that coal ash can be used as a **cementitious or pozzolanic constituent**, with ASTM C618 covering both pozzolanic and cementitious action, or both [N5-R2][N5-F2]. In practical terms, this means coal ash can help meet sustainability targets while still delivering concrete that is strong, durable, and structurally sound.

## 3) Processing challenges and practical constraints of coal ash

### Variability in composition and consistency
One of the main challenges in processing coal ash is **variability in composition**, which can significantly influence how fly ash behaves as a supplementary cementitious material. The evidence from the Florida structural concrete evaluation notes that variability in **mineralogy and chemical composition** can significantly influence coal ash behavior [N4-F4]. This variability is important because it affects **consistency** and **performance** across different sources, requiring careful specification and quality control to ensure reliable results.

### Contamination risks and clean handling
Contamination is another major constraint. The same Florida evaluation report states that landfilled or ponded fly ash can be comingled with **bottom ash**, **flue-gas desulfurization materials (FGD)**, and **fluidized bed combustion (FBC) fly ashes**, which can increase sulfur content and other impurities [N4-F4]. It also warns that the **form of sulfur** present in harvested coal ash, such as calcium sulfate, calcium sulfite, or sodium/alkali sulfate, can substantially affect performance, even though ASTM C618’s chemical analyses do not identify the form of sulfur [N4-F4]. Excess alkali content is also noted as a concern because it can affect reaction rates and concrete durability [N4-F4]. This means that coal ash processing must be carefully managed to avoid contamination from non-ash materials and to ensure that the chemical composition remains within acceptable limits for cementitious use.

### Technical limitations in blending, curing, and quality control
Processing constraints extend to blending and curing. ASTM C618 and related guidance emphasize that coal ash sources should be controlled to avoid ash from **peaking plants, blended coal, other fuels, precipitator additives, start-up/shutdown phases, wet handling, and non-steady-state operation** [N5-F1]. These restrictions are intended to ensure quality and consistency. The FHWA user guideline adds that only a relatively low percentage of all coal fly ash produced annually is potentially suitable for use in PCC because of these source restrictions [N5-F1]. This highlights a key processing challenge: even though coal ash is abundant, only a fraction is suitable for cement/concrete use due to inconsistent sources and handling conditions.

Blending and quality control are also technically limited. The FHWA guidance notes that fly ash used in concrete should be as **consistent and uniform** as possible and should be monitored by a **QA/QC program** that tests **fineness, loss on ignition, specific gravity, and pozzolanic activity** [N5-F1]. It further states that **prequalification of fly ash sources** is important to ensure consistency across projects, because fly ash from different sources may behave differently [N5-F1]. The durability study on coal bottom ash concrete also emphasizes the need for standardization and the role of exposure-class compliance in concrete performance [N2-F3]. These points show that coal ash processing is not simply a matter of mixing; it requires careful selection, conditioning, testing, and standardization to ensure consistent performance.

### Additional processing considerations
The evidence also indicates that **drying or conditioning** is required for blended cement or ready-mix concrete, and that moisture content can influence entrained air content and air-entraining requirements [N5-F1]. It also notes that finely divided materials may reduce entrained air content, so air content must be maintained through tests and additional admixtures if needed [N5-F1]. This means that coal ash processing must be matched to the concrete mix design and curing conditions to avoid adverse effects on workability and durability.

## 4) Industry standards and typical specifications for coal ash in cementitious materials

### ASTM C618 and related standards
Industry standards for coal ash in cementitious materials are primarily governed by **ASTM C618**, which defines acceptable coal ash types and specifies the requirements for **cementitious or pozzolanic action**, or both [N5-R2][N5-F2]. ASTM C618 covers coal fly ash and raw or calcined natural pozzolan for use in concrete where cementitious or pozzolanic action is desired [N5-F2]. It also defines two classes of fly ash for use in concrete: **Class F**, usually derived from anthracite or bituminous coal, and **Class C**, usually derived from lignite or subbituminous coal [N5-F1][N6-R5]. This classification is central to specification because it determines which ash types are suitable for different applications.

### Physical and chemical requirements
The standard also sets **physical and chemical requirements** for the materials, and specifies testing for **fineness, strength activity index, water requirement, soundness, and autoclave expansion or contraction** [N5-F2]. These tests are used to ensure that the ash meets the necessary performance criteria for use in concrete. ASTM C618 also excludes certain residues such as those from **fluidized bed combustion, burning of municipal solid waste or other refuse with coal, or burning of industrial or municipal solid waste in incinerators** [N5-F2]. This exclusion is important because it limits the scope of acceptable coal ash to those that are chemically and physically compatible with cementitious use.

### How standards affect specification, grading, and use limits
The standard’s requirements affect specification, grading, and use limits in several ways. First, ASTM C618 distinguishes between **pozzolanic** and **cementitious action**, which means that different ash types may be used for different applications [N5-F2]. Second, the standard requires **consistent and uniform material**, with quality control through sampling, testing, and prequalification programs [N5-F1]. This means that specification is not only about chemical composition but also about batch-to-batch consistency and source reliability. Third, the standard’s limits on chemical composition and physical properties define acceptable use limits, including limits on **SO₃ content** and other impurities, which are important for avoiding harmful effects on concrete performance [N4-F4].

### Broader applications and blended cement
In addition to raw ash, ASTM C618-related guidance supports **blended cement applications**. ASTM C595 defines blended cement products in which fly ash has been added, including **Portland-pozzolan cement (Type IP)** and **Pozzolan modified Portland cement (Type I-PM)**, with specified percentages of pozzolan [N5-F1]. This shows that the standard framework extends beyond raw ash to blended cement applications, reinforcing the idea that coal ash is regulated not only by its chemical and physical properties but also by how it is incorporated into cementitious systems.

### Classification for specification
The broader evidence also supports the importance of classification for specification. Coal fly ash is classified into **Class C and Class F** based on chemical composition, and bottom ash can meet the **Class F or Class C classification** under ASTM C618 [N6-R3][N6-R4]. This classification is useful for specifying which ash type is suitable for a given mix and for predicting its behavior in concrete. It also explains why ASTM C618 is so important: it provides a common language for specifying acceptable ash types, acceptable action, and acceptable performance.

## 5) Synthesis: what coal ash contributes, and what it requires

Overall, coal ash contributes to cement and concrete production through its **pozzolanic or cementitious activity**, driven by reactive silica, alumina, and calcium oxide content [N5-F1][N1-R2]. It affects hydration by slowing early-age development in Class F ash and potentially enhancing early strength in Class C ash [N5-F1]. It improves long-term strength and durability by reducing permeability, chloride ion penetration, sulfate attack, and drying shrinkage, while still meeting exposure-class requirements [N5-F1][N2-F3]. It also improves workability and reduces shrinkage, making it a valuable material for sustainable concrete production [N5-F1].

The benefits are substantial: **cost savings** through lower material and disposal expenses, **environmental advantages** from waste reuse and reduced emissions, and **performance improvements** such as enhanced durability, reduced permeability, and improved workability [N3-R1][N3-R3][N5-F1]. At the same time, coal ash processing is constrained by **variability in composition**, **contamination risks**, and **technical limitations in blending, curing, and quality control** [N4-F4][N5-F1]. These constraints must be managed through careful source control, conditioning, testing, and standardization to maximize the benefits of coal ash [N5-F1][N5-F2].

In short, coal ash is a versatile and increasingly important material in cementitious systems. It contributes chemically and functionally by replacing part of the cement content and improving durability, while its benefits extend to cost, supply, environmental, and performance advantages. However, those benefits are only realized if the ash is processed and specified carefully, using standards like ASTM C618 and managing the practical constraints of variability, contamination, and quality control [N5-R2][N5-F2][N4-F4].

Processing challenges and practical constraints of coal ash

Processing coal ash in cement/concrete is constrained by variability in composition, contamination risks, and technical limitations in blending, curing, and quality control. One major issue is the variability in coal ash composition, which can significantly influence how fly ash behaves as a supplementary cementitious material. The evidence from the Florida structural concrete evaluation notes that variability in mineralogy and chemical composition can significantly influence coal ash behavior [N4-F4]. This variability is important because it affects consistency and performance across different sources, requiring careful specification and quality control to ensure reliable results.

Contamination risks are another major constraint. The same Florida evaluation report states that landfilled or ponded fly ash can be comingled with bottom ash, flue-gas desulfurization materials (FGD), and fluidized bed combustion (FBC) fly ashes, which can increase sulfur content and other impurities [N4-F4]. It also warns that the form of sulfur present in harvested coal ash, such as calcium sulfate, calcium sulfite, or sodium/alkali sulfate, can substantially affect performance, even though ASTM C618’s chemical analyses do not identify the form of sulfur [N4-F4]. Excess alkali content is also noted as a concern because it can affect reaction rates and concrete durability [N4-F4]. This means that coal ash processing must be carefully managed to avoid contamination from non-ash materials and to ensure that the chemical composition remains within acceptable limits for cementitious use.

The evidence also points to practical handling requirements. ASTM C618 and related guidance emphasize that coal ash sources should be controlled to avoid ash from peaking plants, blended coal, other fuels, precipitator additives, start-up/shutdown phases, wet handling, and non-steady-state operation [N5-F1]. These restrictions are intended to ensure quality and consistency. The FHWA user guideline adds that only a relatively low percentage of all coal fly ash produced annually is potentially suitable for use in PCC because of these source restrictions [N5-F1]. This highlights a key processing challenge: even though coal ash is abundant, only a fraction is suitable for cement/concrete use due to inconsistent sources and handling conditions.

Blending and quality control are also technically limited. The FHWA guidance notes that fly ash used in concrete should be as consistent and uniform as possible and should be monitored by a QA/QC program that tests fineness, loss on ignition, specific gravity, and pozzolanic activity [N5-F1]. It further states that prequalification of fly ash sources is important to ensure consistency across projects, because fly ash from different sources may behave differently [N5-F1]. The durability study on coal bottom ash concrete also emphasizes the need for standardization and the role of exposure-class compliance in concrete performance [N2-F3]. These points show that coal ash processing is not simply a matter of mixing; it requires careful selection, conditioning, testing, and quality assurance to ensure consistent performance.

The evidence indicates that drying or conditioning is required for blended cement or ready-mix concrete, and that moisture content can influence entrained air content and air-entraining requirements [N5-F1]. Industry standards for coal ash in cementitious materials are primarily governed by ASTM C618, which defines acceptable coal ash types and specifies the requirements for cementitious or pozzolanic action. It also defines two classes of fly ash for use in concrete: Class F, usually derived from anthracite or bituminous coal, and Class C, usually derived from lignite or subbituminous coal [N5-F1][N6-R5]. This classification is central to specification because it determines which ash types are suitable for different applications.

The standard also sets physical and chemical requirements for the materials, and specifies testing for fineness, strength activity index, water requirement, soundness, and autoclave expansion or contraction [N5-F2]. These tests are used to ensure that the ash meets the necessary performance criteria for use in concrete. ASTM C618 also excludes certain residues such as those from fluidized bed combustion, burning of municipal solid waste or other refuse with coal, or burning of industrial or municipal solid waste in incinerators [N5-F2]. This exclusion is important because it limits the scope of acceptable coal ash to those that are chemically and physically compatible with cementitious use.

The standard’s requirements affect specification, grading, and use limits in several ways. First, ASTM C618 distinguishes between pozzolanic and cementitious action, which means that different ash types may be used for different applications. Class F ash is pozzolanic, with little or no cementing value alone, while Class C ash has self-cementing properties in addition to pozzolanic properties [N5-F1][N6-R5]. Second, the standard requires consistent and uniform material, with quality control through sampling, testing, and prequalification programs [N5-F1]. This means that specification is not only about chemical composition but also about batch-to-batch consistency and source reliability. Third, the standard’s limits on chemical composition and physical properties define acceptable use limits, including limits on SO₃ content and other impurities, which are important for avoiding harmful effects on concrete performance [N4-F4].

ASTM C595 defines blended cement products in which fly ash has been added, including Portland-pozzolan cement (Type IP) and Pozzolan modified Portland cement (Type I-PM), with specified percentages of pozzolan [N5-F1]. Coal fly ash is classified into Class C and Class F based on chemical composition, and bottom ash can meet the Class F or Class C classification under ASTM C618 [N6-R3][N6-R4]. This classification is useful for specifying which ash type is suitable for a given mix and for predicting its behavior in concrete. It also explains why ASTM C618 is so important: it provides a common language for specifying acceptable ash types, acceptable action, and acceptable performance.

The standards set physical and chemical requirements, test procedures, and exclusion criteria, which together determine specification, grading, and use limits [N5-F2]. They also support blended cement applications and emphasize consistency, source control, and quality assurance, ensuring that coal ash can be used reliably in cementitious materials [N5-F1][N5-F2].

One of the main benefits of coal ash is that it is often a **lower-cost alternative** to raw materials because it is a byproduct of coal combustion rather than a primary ingredient. The evidence notes that fly ash reuse can help reduce environmental impacts, and that reusing fly ash can reduce environmental impacts and lower the cost of disposal [N3-R1][N3-R3]. The durability study on coal bottom ash concrete also highlights that standardization of coal bottom ash as a cement constituent can reduce near-zero cement cost by about 500 €/t, showing a substantial cost advantage [N2-F3]. This makes coal ash attractive not only as a waste stream but also as a way to lower material costs and improve the economic viability of concrete production.

### Environmental benefits
Coal ash reuse offers strong environmental benefits. It reduces the need for **landfill disposal**, helps mitigate **climate change**, and supports **circular economy goals**. The evidence explicitly links fly ash reuse to reduced greenhouse gas emissions, reduced disposal costs, and improved strength and durability [N3-R3]. It also states that **turning liabilities into opportunities** highlights the use of coal ash to reduce the carbon footprint, and that harvested ash can provide environmental benefits for all harvesting processes evaluated [N3-R2][N3-R5]. The durability study similarly emphasizes that coal bottom ash is included in the EU Standardization Request and supports climate change mitigation and low-carbon cement development [N2-F3]. These benefits are particularly important because they show that coal ash can simultaneously reduce emissions, lower waste management costs, and support sustainable construction.

### Performance benefits
Performance benefits are also significant. Coal ash improves concrete durability by reducing **permeability**, **chloride ion penetration**, **sulfate attack**, and **alkali-aggregate reactivity**, while also reducing **drying shrinkage** and **heat of hydration** [N5-F1]. The durability study on coal bottom ash concrete found that CBA-based concretes met water penetration requirements for all exposure classes, which is a strong indicator of long-term durability [N2-F3]. The evidence also notes that coal ash can improve the strength and durability of products using it [N3-R3], and that replacing cement with harvested ash provides environmental benefits [N3-R5]. These performance advantages are important because they mean that coal ash can be used to produce more durable, less permeable concrete without compromising strength or exposure-class compliance.

### Support for low-clinker cement
A related benefit is that coal ash can help support the development of **low-clinker cement**. The durability study notes that reducing the clinker factor is a cheaper supporting measure for climate change mitigation, and that coal bottom ash can be used in blended cements to achieve this goal [N2-F3]. This aligns with the broader evidence that coal ash can be used as a **cementitious or pozzolanic constituent**, with ASTM C618 covering both pozzolanic and cementitious action, or both [N5-R2][N5-F2]. In practical terms, this means coal ash can help meet sustainability targets while still delivering concrete that is strong, durable, and structurally sound.

## 3) Processing challenges and practical constraints of coal ash

### Variability in composition and consistency
One of the main challenges in processing coal ash is **variability in composition**, which can significantly influence how fly ash behaves as a supplementary cementitious material. The evidence from the Florida structural concrete evaluation notes that variability in **mineralogy and chemical composition** can significantly influence coal ash behavior [N4-F4]. This variability is important because it affects **consistency** and **performance** across different sources, requiring careful specification and quality control to ensure reliable results.

### Contamination risks and clean handling
Contamination is another major constraint. The same Florida evaluation report states that landfilled or ponded fly ash can be comingled with **bottom ash**, **flue-gas desulfurization materials (FGD)**, and **fluidized bed combustion (FBC) fly ashes**, which can increase sulfur content and other impurities [N4-F4]. It also warns that the **form of sulfur** present in harvested coal ash, such as calcium sulfate, calcium sulfite, or sodium/alkali sulfate, can substantially affect performance, even though ASTM C618’s chemical analyses do not identify the form of sulfur [N4-F4]. Excess alkali content is also noted as a concern because it can affect reaction rates and concrete durability [N4-F4]. This means that coal ash processing must be carefully managed to avoid contamination from non-ash materials and to ensure that the chemical composition remains within acceptable limits for cementitious use.

### Technical limitations in blending, curing, and quality control
Processing constraints extend to blending and curing. ASTM C618 and related guidance emphasize that coal ash sources should be controlled to avoid ash from **peaking plants, blended coal, other fuels, precipitator additives, start-up/shutdown phases, wet handling, and non-steady-state operation** [N5-F1]. These restrictions are intended to ensure quality and consistency. The FHWA user guideline adds that only a relatively low percentage of all coal fly ash produced annually is potentially suitable for use in PCC because of these source restrictions [N5-F1]. This highlights a key processing challenge: even though coal ash is abundant, only a fraction is suitable for cement/concrete use due to inconsistent sources and handling conditions.

Blending and quality control are also technically limited. The FHWA guidance notes that fly ash used in concrete should be as **consistent and uniform** as possible and should be monitored by a **QA/QC program** that tests **fineness, loss on ignition, specific gravity, and pozzolanic activity** [N5-F1]. It further states that **prequalification of fly ash sources** is important to ensure consistency across projects, because fly ash from different sources may behave differently [N5-F1]. The durability study on coal bottom ash concrete also emphasizes the need for standardization and the role of exposure-class compliance in concrete performance [N2-F3]. These points show that coal ash processing is not simply a matter of mixing; it requires careful selection, conditioning, testing, and standardization to ensure consistent performance.

### Additional processing considerations
The evidence also indicates that **drying or conditioning** is required for blended cement or ready-mix concrete, and that moisture content can influence entrained air content and air-entraining requirements [N5-F1]. It also notes that finely divided materials may reduce entrained air content, so air content must be maintained through tests and additional admixtures if needed [N5-F1]. This means that coal ash processing must be matched to the concrete mix design and curing conditions to avoid adverse effects on workability and durability.

## 4) Industry standards and typical specifications for coal ash in cementitious materials

### ASTM C618 and related standards
Industry standards for coal ash in cementitious materials are primarily governed by **ASTM C618**, which defines acceptable coal ash types and specifies the requirements for **cementitious or pozzolanic action**, or both [N5-R2][N5-F2]. ASTM C618 covers coal fly ash and raw or calcined natural pozzolan for use in concrete where cementitious or pozzolanic action is desired [N5-F2]. It also defines two classes of fly ash for use in concrete: **Class F**, usually derived from anthracite or bituminous coal, and **Class C**, usually derived from lignite or subbituminous coal [N5-F1][N6-R5]. This classification is central to specification because it determines which ash types are suitable for different applications.

### Physical and chemical requirements
The standard also sets **physical and chemical requirements** for the materials, and specifies testing for **fineness, strength activity index, water requirement, soundness, and autoclave expansion or contraction** [N5-F2]. These tests are used to ensure that the ash meets the necessary performance criteria for use in concrete. ASTM C618 also excludes certain residues such as those from **fluidized bed combustion, burning of municipal solid waste or other refuse with coal, or burning of industrial or municipal solid waste in incinerators** [N5-F2]. This exclusion is important because it limits the scope of acceptable coal ash to those that are chemically and physically compatible with cementitious use.

### How standards affect specification, grading, and use limits
The standard’s requirements affect specification, grading, and use limits in several ways. First, ASTM C618 distinguishes between **pozzolanic** and **cementitious action**, which means that different ash types may be used for different applications [N5-F2]. Second, the standard requires **consistent and uniform material**, with quality control through sampling, testing, and prequalification programs [N5-F1]. This means that specification is not only about chemical composition but also about batch-to-batch consistency and source reliability. Third, the standard’s limits on chemical composition and physical properties define acceptable use limits, including limits on **SO₃ content** and other impurities, which are important for avoiding harmful effects on concrete performance [N4-F4].

### Broader applications and blended cement
In addition to raw ash, ASTM C618-related guidance supports **blended cement applications**. ASTM C595 defines blended cement products in which fly ash has been added, including **Portland-pozzolan cement (Type IP)** and **Pozzolan modified Portland cement (Type I-PM)**, with specified percentages of pozzolan [N5-F1]. This shows that the standard framework extends beyond raw ash to blended cement applications, reinforcing the idea that coal ash is regulated not only by its chemical and physical properties but also by how it is incorporated into cementitious systems.

### Classification for specification
The broader evidence also supports the importance of classification for specification. Coal fly ash is classified into **Class C and Class F** based on chemical composition, and bottom ash can meet the **Class F or Class C classification** under ASTM C618 [N6-R3][N6-R4]. This classification is useful for specifying which ash type is suitable for a given mix and for predicting its behavior in concrete. It also explains why ASTM C618 is so important: it provides a common language for specifying acceptable ash types, acceptable action, and acceptable performance.

## 5) Synthesis: what coal ash contributes, and what it requires

Overall, coal ash contributes to cement and concrete production through its **pozzolanic or cementitious activity**, driven by reactive silica, alumina, and calcium oxide content [N5-F1][N1-R2]. It affects hydration by slowing early-age development in Class F ash and potentially enhancing early strength in Class C ash [N5-F1]. It improves long-term strength and durability by reducing permeability, chloride ion penetration, sulfate attack, and drying shrinkage, while still meeting exposure-class requirements [N5-F1][N2-F3]. It also improves workability and reduces shrinkage, making it a valuable material for sustainable concrete production [N5-F1].

The benefits are substantial: **cost savings** through lower material and disposal expenses, **environmental advantages** from waste reuse and reduced emissions, and **performance improvements** such as enhanced durability, reduced permeability, and improved workability [N3-R1][N3-R3][N5-F1]. At the same time, coal ash processing is constrained by **variability in composition**, **contamination risks**, and **technical limitations in blending, curing, and quality control** [N4-F4][N5-F1]. These constraints must be managed through careful source control, conditioning, testing, and standardization to maximize the benefits of coal ash [N5-F1][N5-F2].

In short, coal ash is a versatile and increasingly important material in cementitious systems. It contributes chemically and functionally by replacing part of the cement content and improving durability, while its benefits extend to cost, supply, environmental, and performance advantages. However, those benefits are only realized if the ash is processed and specified carefully, using standards like ASTM C618 and managing the practical constraints of variability, contamination, and quality control [N5-R2][N5-F2][N4-F4].
